title: [Suite autour de Teichmüller dont] Teichmülleries, 1981-1982 : notes manuscrites (1981-1983, s.d.), lettres (1981, s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
Item 9 of notes recording conversations, apparently with Deligne. The topic is when a cone, or a link in a stratified space, can be a manifold without the link being a sphere. The concern serves Grothendieck's programme on 'cartes' (combinatorial maps) and stratified or polyhedral structures. In particular he wants topological conditions on a conical stratification that would force certain links to be spheres; item 10 on the next page treats regular maps and Coxeter groups.

The example, in modern terms:
- Let Γ ⊂ S^3 = SU(2) be the binary icosahedral group, of order 120. It is the preimage of A_5 ⊂ SO(3,R) = S^3/{±1}.
- Then P = S^3/Γ ≅ SO(3)/A_5 is the Poincaré homology sphere. Grothendieck describes it nicely as the space of regular icosahedra inscribed in a given sphere.
- P is not a sphere, since π1 = Γ ≠ 1.
- Its suspension ΣP is not a manifold. At the two suspension points the local fundamental group (π1 of the deleted neighbourhood) is Γ, which is non-trivial.
- Yet ΣP is a simply connected compact space.
- ΣP × R is a manifold (Edwards).
- The double suspension Σ²P ≅ S^5 is a manifold, including at the two 'poles'. Grothendieck flags the uncertain steps with '(?)'.
- Hence the open cone on S = ΣP, which is ≅ c(P) × R ≅ R^5, is a manifold although S is not even a manifold, let alone a sphere.

The margin records the general theorem with its reference: if X is an n-dimensional homology sphere, then its double suspension is a sphere. This is the Edwards–Cannon double suspension theorem, cited via the Séminaire Bourbaki 1977-78, exposé 515.

The last paragraph reports Deligne's view. To state topological conditions on a space (a conical stratification) that imply that certain links are spheres, one must work in a PL-type framework; the next page adds 'or better ones, à la Thurston', because the purely topological condition does not lend itself to this. Grothendieck adds a hope, to be checked carefully, that for locally finite regular 'cartes' the difficulties disappear.
errors: The opening sentence says 'le cône sur une variété compacte S'. If S is a compact manifold whose open cone is a manifold, then S is a simply connected homology sphere, hence a homotopy sphere. So S is a sphere modulo the Poincaré conjecture (open in dimension 3 in 1981-82). Grothendieck's own example uses S = ΣP, which is not a manifold. He partly corrects this further down by replacing the wording with 'espace simplement connexe S'.

The sentence about the suspension is syntactically garbled ('Mais c'est un espace simplement connexe S'). The intended argument is that ΣP is simply connected, its cone or its product with R is a manifold, and its double suspension is a sphere. The '(?)' marks show that Grothendieck was unsure, but the claims are correct by Edwards–Cannon.

ideas.what: Poincaré homology sphere realised as S^3/binary icosahedral group ≅ SO(3)/A_5 ≅ space of regular icosahedra inscribed in a sphere
ideas.usually_credited_to: Poincaré (1904); the quotient description is classical (Threlfall–Seifert, Kirby–Scharlemann 'Eight faces')

ideas.what: Suspension of the Poincaré sphere is not a manifold (local π1 = Γ at the suspension points), but its product with R, its cone, and its double suspension are manifolds
ideas.usually_credited_to: R. D. Edwards (1975-77), J. W. Cannon (1978-79); exposé: F. Latour, Sém. Bourbaki 1977/78 no. 515

ideas.what: Need for a PL (or Thurston-type) framework to give conditions on conical stratifications forcing links to be spheres; hope that locally finite regular 'cartes' avoid the difficulties
ideas.modern_name: Recognition of manifolds / links in stratified (PL) spaces; regular CW or polyhedral complexes
ideas.usually_credited_to: Cannon (recognition problem), Edwards; PL topology tradition
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme discusses 'cartes', tame topology and stratified structures, but not this specific point

deep.surprise_reason: The page summarises a well-known theorem (Edwards–Cannon double suspension) with the standard example and its Bourbaki reference. The only distinctive touches are the 'space of inscribed regular icosahedra' description and its placement within Grothendieck's motivation of tame or stratified topology for 'cartes'. There is nothing new.
transcription_corrections: Margin '(Cannon, 515)' is very likely '(Latour, 515)': F. Latour, 'Double suspension d'une sphère d'homologie [d'après R. Edwards]', Séminaire Bourbaki 1977/78, exposé 515.

'$\mathfrak{A}_5^+ \subset S^3/\pm 1$': the image shows $\mathfrak{A}_5 \subset S^3/\pm1$ with $\mathfrak{A}$ written underneath as an abbreviation and 'SO(3,R)' under $S^3/\pm1$; there is no '+' superscript intended.
'sa {+double+}[?] suspension est une variété': the context (the margin and the 'deux pôles') supports 'double suspension'.
The inserted phrase '{+de licité[?] de structure top.[?] polyg.[?]+}' is uncertain; it may read 'd'unicité de structure top./polyg.' or similar.
'considérons le [?]-groupe' is probably 'le sous-groupe' (the binary icosahedral subgroup).
